articles.title: From teaching assistant to PT: how Rochdale mum Jen Daker found the strongest version of herself
articles.excerpt: After 16 years in education, mum-of-two Jen Daker has found a new calling as a personal trainer at The Hybrid Hut in Rochdale, combining 4am discipline, family life and a passion for helping others build confidence.
articles.content_html:
There is an obvious physical transformation in Jen Daker’s story.

She is in the best shape of her life, trains with formidable discipline and has built a new career around fitness.

But Jen’s transformation goes far beyond how she looks.

For 16 years, Jen worked at the same school as a teaching assistant. She loved education, loved working with children and, for most of her adult working life, it was all she had known.

Then she became a mum.

After two pregnancies, her priorities began to change. Fitness, which had always been part of her life, became increasingly important not simply for how she looked, but for how she felt.

“I loved working in education, but after having children my priorities changed,” she said. “Fitness helped me so much physically and mentally after two pregnancies. I realised that if I could help other people feel like that, that was what I wanted to do.”

At 36, with two young children and a mortgage, changing careers was not the easy option.

Jen did it anyway.

Today she is a personal trainer at The Hybrid Hut in Rochdale, working with women and men of different ages, abilities and levels of confidence.

At the heart of her approach is one simple principle: consistency matters more than perfection.

Jen gets up at 4am to train.

There are mornings when staying in bed would be considerably easier, particularly after a broken night with the children.

But before school runs, clients, work and everything else involved in raising a family begins, Jen deliberately creates time that belongs to her.

“My workout isn’t just about keeping fit — it’s my time,” she said. “Before the school runs, work and everything else that comes with being a mum, I get an hour that’s just for me.”

Training first thing sets the tone for the rest of her day. She feels more energetic, her mood improves and she has already done something positive for herself before everybody else begins needing her.

It is an impressive level of discipline, but Jen is quick to point out that she does not wake every morning overflowing with motivation.

“Motivation comes and goes, but habits keep you going,” she said. “Some workouts are amazing and some aren’t. Showing up is what matters.”

That is also what she wants her clients to understand.

A healthy life is not built from one heroic gym session or one perfect week.

It is built from the ordinary things repeated often enough to matter. One walk. One healthier meal. One short workout. Then another.

Jen is equally clear that she did not make such a dramatic change alone.

Behind the early mornings, late evenings and weekend sessions is a family finding ways to make it work — and she credits her partner Damien as one of the central reasons she has been able to pursue it.

“I honestly couldn’t have made such a huge career change at 36, with two young children and a mortgage, without Damien,” she said.

“There are early mornings, late evenings and weekends where we’re juggling family life around work. Having someone who believes in you, encourages you and helps share the load makes such a difference.”

Her family, she says, have supported her from day one.

That strong relationship with Damien and her obvious love for her children sit at the centre of the life she has built rather than competing with it.

Jen does not pretend the balance is effortless. Some weeks work better than others.

“I’m still figuring it out,” she said. “I’ve learnt that looking after myself isn’t selfish — it’s necessary.”

Sometimes that means a workout. Sometimes a walk. Sometimes simply finding enough time for a quiet coffee.

For Jen, exercise has increasingly become about mental wellbeing.

She describes herself as having an active mind and says she can struggle to switch off. Exercise creates headspace.

“Life can feel hectic with work and children, and training gives me time to reset,” she said.

“It’s helped build my confidence and resilience. I don’t exercise because I want to look a certain way anymore. I do it because I know how much better I feel mentally when I move my body.”

But even someone capable of getting out of bed at 4am has had to learn that discipline is not the same thing as endlessly pushing harder.

There have been days when Jen has been exhausted or overwhelmed and recognised that another intense workout was not what her body needed.

Sometimes the healthier choice is a walk. Sometimes stretching. Sometimes rest.

“Listening to your body is just as important as pushing yourself,” she said. “Fitness should support your wellbeing, not become another source of pressure.”

She admits she is still learning to follow that advice herself.

Jen’s attitude towards food is similarly grounded in real life.

She loves food. Nothing is completely off limits.

And she does not want clients spending their lives bouncing between restrictive diets and guilt.

Her philosophy is that a healthy lifestyle must still leave room for birthdays, holidays, meals out and the foods people genuinely enjoy.

“One meal or one night out doesn’t undo months of healthy habits, just like one salad doesn’t suddenly make someone healthy,” she said.

“Food shouldn’t come with guilt.”

Instead, Jen encourages moderation and habits people can realistically sustain.

“Consistency wins every time. It’s what you do most of the time that matters, not what you do occasionally.

“Celebrate birthdays, enjoy holidays and make memories. Then just get back to your normal routine afterwards.”

There is no waiting for Monday. No declaring the month ruined because of one bad day.

“It’s never too late to start again,” Jen said. “Make your next choice a positive one and keep moving forward.”

Some of Jen’s proudest results cannot be measured with scales or photographed in a mirror.

One of her earliest clients found her after seeing a recommendation on Facebook. The pair had never met.

The woman had never even been inside a gym and arrived nervous and lacking confidence.

Over time, that changed. She began trusting herself. She became comfortable training. Eventually, while Jen was away on holiday, she went to the gym on her own — something she once would never have imagined doing.

“She is like a totally different person to the woman I met,” Jen said.

For Jen, that is the real reward.

“I’ve met people who were scared to walk into a gym become confident enough to train on their own,” she said.

“Most of the time the biggest transformation isn’t physical — it’s the confidence they gain in every part of their lives.”

She sees that particularly among mothers.

Motherhood can be all-consuming. Somewhere among school runs, work, washing, appointments and everybody else’s needs, women can begin feeling that the person they once were has disappeared.

Jen understands that. And she loves watching them find themselves again.

There is another misconception Jen would happily dismantle: that personal trainers are endlessly confident.

She believes the reality can be almost the opposite.

Working every day in an environment where bodies and physical performance are constantly visible can make trainers highly critical of themselves if they allow it.

And they certainly are not expecting new clients to arrive already fit.

“Most trainers just want to help people improve, whatever their starting point is,” she said.

Jen even experienced nerves herself after recently returning from a two-week holiday.

“I got the pre-gym nerves going back,” she said.

Her message to somebody frightened of walking into a gym for the first time is straightforward. Almost everybody has felt like that. Most other people are concentrating on their own workout, not watching yours.

“Every confident person in the gym was a beginner once,” Jen said. “The hardest part is walking through the door.”

There is perhaps no such thing as perfectly balancing motherhood, relationships, work, health, friendships and everything else expected of women.

Some days one thing will inevitably win.

But Jen Daker’s story suggests women can get remarkably close.

Today, Jen offers one-to-one personal training, small-group sessions and tailored online fitness plans, working with people of all ages and abilities.

She describes The Hybrid Hut as a gym where beginners, experienced athletes, younger people and older clients are all equally welcome.

Train with Jen Daker at The Hybrid Hut.

The Hybrid Hut, Unit 1A, Moss Mill Street / Woodbine Street East Industrial Estate, Rochdale, OL16 5LB. Telephone: 07547 619709. Jen can also be contacted through her Instagram and Facebook pages, or by visiting The Hybrid Hut in Rochdale.

articles.title: WellMental UK hosts first men's mental health fitness session in Heywood
articles.excerpt: WellMental UK held its first session in Heywood on Friday evening, combining fitness, food and conversation to support men's mental health.
articles.content_html:
WellMental UK hosted its first men's mental health fitness session in Heywood on Friday evening, bringing local men together for exercise, food and conversation.

The session took place at Unit4 Fitness and began with a group workout before moving into a relaxed social evening. Attendees shared a curry, spent time together and were encouraged to talk openly in an informal setting.

Organisers said it was encouraging to see those attending getting involved, supporting one another and making the most of the opportunity to spend time together.

The event was designed to combine physical activity with peer support and conversation, creating a space where men could connect without the pressure of a formal clinical environment.

WellMental UK thanked everyone who attended and helped make the first Heywood session a success.

The evening marked the beginning of the group's activity in Heywood, with the first session focused on building community, encouraging openness and using fitness as a way to bring people together.

articles.title: Homelessness, addiction and the cruelty of public condemnation
articles.excerpt: A disabled homeless man outside Tesco Express on Whitworth Road has become the subject of photographs, insults and jokes online. The harder question is whether public humiliation solves anything at all.
articles.content_html:
There is a homeless man who regularly sits outside Tesco Express on Whitworth Road in Rochdale. He uses a wheelchair, has one leg, and appears to have longstanding problems with drug dependency. In recent days, photographs purporting to show him using drugs have been circulated in a local social-media group, accompanied by descriptions including ‘junkie’, ‘scruff’ and ‘down and out’, together with jokes about his disability.

Those comments deserve more scrutiny than the man they were aimed at.

It is entirely legitimate for residents to object to public drug use, theft, abusive behaviour or intimidation. It is legitimate for shop workers to expect protection at work. It is legitimate for parents to dislike exposing children to distressing scenes. But there is a clear moral distinction between criticising behaviour and publicly degrading a vulnerable person. Calling a homeless, disabled man a ‘scruff’ does not protect children. Making jokes about his missing leg does not reduce drug use. Posting photographs of him at what may be one of the lowest points of his life does not help shop staff, improve public safety or increase the likelihood that he enters treatment. It serves a different purpose: humiliation.

The ease with which some people have participated in that humiliation should trouble us.

The editor of Rochdale Daily has spoken to this man several times. In those encounters, he has not demanded money. He has generally asked for a drink, usually a chocolate milkshake. Other residents have independently described similar experiences. A Tesco worker has, by contrast, said that staff sometimes experience him as abusive. Both accounts may be true. Addiction, withdrawal, mental distress and homelessness do not produce consistent behaviour.

That does not make abuse acceptable. But neither does difficult behaviour grant the public permission to strip somebody of dignity.

During one conversation, the man said he had previously been prescribed methadone but stopped collecting it because he felt demeaned and discriminated against when attending the dispensing pharmacy. Rochdale Daily has not independently verified that account. When asked whether he would consider restarting treatment if his medication could be dispensed somewhere he felt able to attend, he said yes.

That exchange should matter more than a photograph. It suggests that beneath the visible disorder is a person who can still discuss treatment, medication and the possibility of changing his circumstances. Yet this is precisely the sort of person whom public discussion can rapidly reduce to a caricature. Once the word ‘junkie’ has been applied, the individual disappears and only the label remains. That is not analysis. It is intellectual laziness.

Addiction is not a mysterious condition. It is extensively studied, medically recognised and strongly associated with homelessness, trauma, mental ill-health and social exclusion. National treatment statistics show that among people entering treatment for opiate problems in England in 2024–25, 41 per cent had no home of their own and 10 per cent were sleeping rough. Government research into rough sleeping published in 2025 found that 54 per cent of respondents reported a drug or alcohol misuse need during the preceding year.

These figures do not excuse criminal or antisocial behaviour. They do, however, make a mockery of the idea that addiction can be solved by simply telling somebody to ‘sort themselves out’. A person who is homeless must try to recover without privacy, stability, reliable sleep, secure storage, regular meals or often even basic hygiene. They may need to attend treatment, collect prescriptions, keep appointments, manage benefits, maintain identification documents and navigate housing applications while sleeping outside. To describe failure under those conditions as proof of moral inferiority is not toughness. It is ignorance.

One comment in the local discussion suggested that drug users should do these things ‘behind their own doors’. That statement is revealing precisely because the man in question does not have one.

Most people have the privilege of experiencing their worst behaviour privately. They can drink too much behind curtains, suffer mental-health crises in bedrooms, argue with family in kitchens, withdraw from medication under a duvet or make disastrous decisions without a stranger photographing them. A rough sleeper does not have a private sphere. His bedroom is public. His living room is public. His breakdowns are public. His addiction is public. And then the same society that has left him without a private space condemns him for failing to keep his problems out of sight. There is something deeply incoherent about that.

The man's disability makes the tone of some comments particularly ugly. Government research published in 2025 found that 80 per cent of people surveyed while sleeping rough reported a longstanding physical impairment, illness or disability. Yet a local discussion about a homeless man with one leg included jokes about his wheelchair. There is no serious public-interest argument for that. It is not community safety. It is not concern for children. It is not anger about shoplifting. It is mockery of disability, and adults should be capable of naming that for what it is.

The same applies to language such as ‘scruff’ and ‘down and out’. Such terms do not describe conduct; they reduce a person to a social category deemed beneath respect. The implication is that once somebody becomes sufficiently poor, addicted or visibly disordered, ordinary standards of human decency no longer apply to the way we speak about them. That proposition should be rejected. A person's entitlement to dignity cannot depend upon whether they are pleasant enough, clean enough, sober enough or useful enough to satisfy strangers on Facebook.

Rochdale also needs to confront the practical context. The borough is already under intense housing pressure. Under Places for Everyone, Rochdale's housing requirement for 2025 to 2030 is 616 homes per year. Council material from 2025 recorded 7,681 applicants on the housing register, while more recent council reporting has referred to approximately 20,000 people relying upon the register and nearly 7,500 meeting statutory ‘reasonable preference’ criteria. Rochdale Council declared a housing emergency in 2023.

So the instruction often directed at people like this man is effectively the following: become sober, become stable, engage with treatment, organise your paperwork, maintain appointments, secure benefits and compete for scarce housing, all while sleeping outside and managing a major physical disability. That is not impossible. But anyone describing it as simple has probably never attempted anything remotely comparable.

There are also legal considerations when photographs and allegations are published online. Taking a photograph in a public place is not automatically unlawful, and Rochdale Daily is not suggesting otherwise. Identifiable images can, depending on context, constitute personal data, while publishing a photograph alongside a serious allegation of criminal behaviour raises separate legal questions.

The Defamation Act 2013 provides protection against statements that cause or are likely to cause serious reputational harm. Truth may be a defence, but that is different from saying that anything alleged on social media is lawful merely because the publisher believes it. If an identifiable photograph is accompanied by an assertion that a person is committing a criminal offence, the publisher should be in a position to substantiate what is being alleged. Rochdale Daily is therefore not independently stating that the man was consuming a Class A drug based solely on photographs and comments circulated online.

There is an additional point that some contributors may wish to consider before reaching for the camera. Vulnerability does not make somebody public property. The fact that a person's suffering occurs on a pavement does not create an entitlement to turn it into entertainment, gossip or a community spectacle. There may be circumstances in which photographing suspected criminal behaviour serves a legitimate evidential purpose. There is a substantial difference between preserving evidence for police and distributing an image among neighbours so that strangers can compete to produce the most contemptuous description of the person depicted. One is potentially evidence gathering. The other can become a form of public shaming.

And public shaming has a cost. If a person already believes that institutions regard him as worthless, if he already feels humiliated collecting treatment, if strangers photograph him and hundreds of neighbours discuss whether he is a ‘scruff’, then it should not surprise anyone if disengagement, isolation and further drug use follow. People sometimes ask why addicts do not seek help while simultaneously creating a social environment in which admitting addiction results in contempt. They demand recovery while reinforcing shame. They demand engagement while making the person feel despised. They demand that somebody rejoin society while making it clear that society would rather not look at them. Those positions are difficult to reconcile.

There is also a tendency to present compassion as naïveté. Those who have defended the man have been dismissed as ‘Karens’ or ‘do gooders’, as though refusing to join in public degradation demonstrates some failure to understand the realities of addiction. The opposite may be true. It requires very little sophistication to dislike someone behaving badly in public. It requires considerably more maturity to condemn the behaviour without enjoying the destruction of the person.

Compassion does not mean giving unlimited money to somebody with an addiction. It does not mean ignoring theft. It does not mean expecting retail workers to endure abuse. It does not mean pretending crack cocaine is harmless. It means retaining the ability to distinguish a human being from his worst behaviour. That distinction is central to every serious approach to rehabilitation.

If society genuinely wants people to recover from addiction, then those people must eventually be able to imagine themselves as something other than an addict. If every interaction reinforces that they are disgusting, worthless and permanently defined by their dependency, society should not be surprised when they behave as though there is little left to recover.

Rochdale Council lists homelessness support, drug and alcohol treatment and specialist services including Turning Point. Those services are important, but complex cases require coordination. A homeless person with a major physical disability and drug dependency may simultaneously require healthcare, treatment, medication management, benefits assistance, housing support and persistent outreach. That is difficult work. Writing ‘absolute scruff’ beneath a photograph is considerably easier. Perhaps that is part of its appeal. It allows people to experience the satisfaction of condemning a social problem without undertaking any of the difficult work involved in solving it.

There is a legitimate debate to be had about public drug use in Rochdale. There is a legitimate debate about homelessness, shoplifting, antisocial behaviour, policing, treatment capacity and the availability of supported accommodation. Those are serious subjects. Wheelchair jokes are not. Photographing a visibly vulnerable disabled man for the purpose of ridicule is not. Describing somebody at the lowest point of his life as though he were vermin contributes nothing whatsoever to the safety or wellbeing of Rochdale.

Residents are entitled to expect streets that are safe and usable. Tesco staff are entitled to work without abuse. Children should not have to encounter dangerous drug paraphernalia. Police should deal with offences where offences occur. But none of those propositions requires cruelty.

The question for Rochdale is not whether this man is admirable. He may not be. The question is whether a civilised community applies standards of dignity only to people whose lives are already in order. Most of the people commenting about him will eventually put their phones down and return home. They will have a bathroom, a bed, heating, a front door and somewhere to make their mistakes privately. He will still be outside. That difference should produce some humility.

If a community cannot look at a homeless, addicted, disabled man without turning his circumstances into entertainment, then there is more than one social problem on display. One is sitting on the pavement. The other is holding the camera.

articles.title: Rochdale businesses urged to back Denehurst House in £30-a-month veterans challenge
articles.excerpt: A Rochdale veterans support organisation is asking 100 local businesses to pledge £30 a month to help keep Denehurst House operational and support former service personnel in need.
articles.content_html:
A Rochdale veterans support organisation has launched a drive to recruit 100 local businesses willing to pledge £30 a month towards keeping Denehurst House operational.

Get Together After Serving CIC, which is behind the campaign, says Denehurst House provides support for veterans including emergency housing, hot meals and mental health support. The organisation is promoting the appeal as the Rochdale 100 Businesses Challenge and is asking firms across the borough to make a regular monthly contribution.

If all 100 places are filled, the campaign would generate £3,000 each month in pledged support, equivalent to £36,000 over a full year if every business remained involved for 12 months. The appeal describes the contribution as a relatively small commitment for an individual business which, collectively, could make a significant difference to the service.

Campaign material highlights community spirit, warm meals and local businesses working together, with the message: 'Together, we keep Denehurst House operational.' It also says the project aims to provide a lifeline to veterans when they need it most.

The initiative is seeking support from companies of all sizes rather than relying on a handful of major donors. That model would spread the cost across the local business community while giving Denehurst House a more predictable stream of recurring income.

Local businesses interested in joining the challenge are being asked to contact Get Together After Serving CIC by emailing hello@gtascic.co.uk.

Rochdale Daily is publishing the appeal as today's front-page community story to help local firms understand what is being requested, how the funding model works and how they can take part.

articles.title: Free food, performances and community activities coming to Rochdale town centre this Saturday
articles.excerpt: Side-by-Side: Feed Our Minds & Souls will bring free performances, creative activities, community conversations, refreshments and 100 free lunch bags to Rochdale town centre on Saturday 15 August.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale town centre will host a full day of free food, performances, creative activities and community connection this Saturday as Side-by-Side: Feed Our Minds & Souls takes place across the town centre.

The event, taking place on Saturday 15 August, is designed around food, community, connection and belonging, with a programme of activities open to residents throughout the day.

Visitors can enjoy free performances, community conversations, creative activities, refreshments and cake, with 100 free lunch bags available for early arrivals.

The programme includes No Such Thing and Story Saturdays, alongside the Wellbeing Zone and Global Café, with organisers promising something for people of all ages to enjoy.

The event forms part of the wider Side-by-Side programme, which is bringing a series of free cultural and community activities into Rochdale town centre this summer.

Families, residents and visitors are encouraged to come along, take part in the activities and spend time connecting with others across the town centre.

Side-by-Side: Feed Our Minds & Souls takes place on Saturday 15 August in Rochdale Town Centre. Further details are available through the organisers' social media channels.

articles.title: One urgent care centre for 220,000 people: does Rochdale not deserve a real hospital?
articles.excerpt: Fifteen years after losing its A&E and maternity unit, Rochdale relies on a minor-injuries urgent care centre while its emergencies travel to Bury, Oldham and Manchester. Research shows distance to emergency care carries a measurable mortality risk.
articles.content_html:
A borough of 220,000 people. One urgent care facility. No A&E, no maternity unit, no children's ward. Is that really adequate for Rochdale?

Rochdale Infirmary is open, and its staff do valuable work. The Whitehall Street site runs a 24/7 Urgent Care Centre, a short-stay Clinical Assessment Unit, day surgery, a rheumatology centre, x-ray, blood testing, antenatal clinics, an early pregnancy unit, outpatient clinics and an eye unit. But the NHS's own description is blunt: there is no A&E at Rochdale Infirmary. The Urgent Care Centre treats minor injury and illness. It is the fourth smallest hospital in the Northern Care Alliance.

That is what remains of a hospital that, within living memory, was a proper district general. The A&E department closed in 2011. The maternity unit went the same way, along with the children's ward and, over the past two decades, ward after ward of acute provision - each removal justified at the time as centralisation, each leaving Rochdale residents travelling further for care.

Today, a Rochdale resident with a genuine emergency is sent to Fairfield in Bury, the Royal Oldham, or North Manchester General. On a good day, that is a manageable journey. In an ambulance queue, at rush hour, or for a family without a car relying on two buses, it is anything but. Every expectant mother in the borough gives birth outside it.

Does distance cost lives? The honest answer is that nobody publishes a Rochdale-specific figure, and we will not invent one. No official body calculates the percentage of local deaths that could have been avoided if a full hospital were closer, and any number we quoted would be guesswork. What does exist is peer-reviewed national research. A study of over 10,000 life-threatening emergency cases, published in the Emergency Medicine Journal by University of Sheffield researchers, found that the risk of death rose as the journey to hospital lengthened - from 5.8% for patients living under 10km away to 8.8% for those more than 20km away, with each additional 10km associated with around a one percentage point increase in mortality. Distance to emergency care is not a neutral fact. It is a clinical risk factor.

That research does not prove any individual Rochdale death was avoidable. It does mean the burden of proof should sit with those who decided that a borough of 220,000 people - larger than many towns and cities with a full district general hospital - can safely be served by a minor injuries facility.

The underuse of the Infirmary compounds the frustration. The site exists. The buildings exist. A workforce exists. Yet its role has been steadily narrowed rather than rebuilt, even as the borough's population has grown and the hospitals absorbing Rochdale's emergencies report some of the longest waits in the country. If capacity across north-east Greater Manchester is the problem - and A&E waiting figures suggest it is - then an under-used hospital estate in the middle of a 220,000-person borough looks less like a rational configuration and more like an inherited decision nobody has had the courage to revisit.

We asked whether the borough's elected representatives have taken a public position on restoring acute services to the Infirmary. We could find no current on-record statements from the borough's MPs or councillors specifically committing to that goal, and rather than paraphrase old campaign material we have chosen to put the question directly: does Rochdale's political leadership believe the current provision is adequate for this borough - and if not, what are they doing about it? We will publish their answers in full.

Fifteen years on from losing its A&E, the question for Rochdale is no longer how the services went, but why a borough this size should not expect them back. A fully equipped hospital - with an emergency department, a maternity unit and the wards this town has lost - is not nostalgia. For 220,000 people, it is the level of provision most comparable boroughs would consider a baseline.

If you are seriously ill or injured, always call 999 or attend your nearest A&E. The Urgent Care Centre at Rochdale Infirmary remains open 24/7 for minor injuries and illness, and NHS 111 can advise on the right service.

articles.title: Rainbow Health Group invites residents to open day at new clinic after 17 years on Hornby Street
articles.excerpt: The health and wellbeing clinic is moving to a new home after 17 years, and is welcoming the community to an open day this Saturday - with the Mayor and Mayoress performing the official opening at 1pm.
articles.content_html:
A local health and wellbeing clinic is inviting Milnrow and Newhey residents - and anyone else who fancies a look around - to celebrate the start of a new chapter this weekend.

After 17 years at its Hornby Street clinic, Rainbow Health Group is moving to a brand-new home, and is holding an open day on Saturday 8 August from 11am to 3pm to welcome the community through the doors.

The clinic offers a range of treatments including sports massage, clinical massage, acupuncture, K-Laser therapy, podiatry and rehabilitation, helping people recover from injuries, manage pain and improve their overall wellbeing.

Its new address is Unit 9A, Southgate Industrial Park, Green Lane, Heywood, OL10 1ND.

Visitors on the day can explore the new clinic, meet the team, and learn more about the treatments and services on offer, with complimentary light refreshments provided. There will also be a charity raffle in aid of Help 4 All, and the Mayor and Mayoress will officially open the clinic at 1pm.

"Whether you've been visiting us for years or have never heard of Rainbow Health Group before, everyone is welcome," the clinic said. "We'd love to see you there and celebrate this exciting new chapter with our local community."

articles.title: Every GP practice in Rochdale ranked by patients in the 2026 survey
articles.excerpt: The latest GP Patient Survey shows a wide gap in reported patient experience between practices across Rochdale, Heywood, Middleton, Littleborough and Milnrow.
articles.content_html:
Patients have rated their experiences at GP practices across Rochdale borough in the latest national survey, revealing a wide difference between the highest and lowest results recorded on one key measure.

Rochdale Daily compared practices using the percentage of respondents who described their overall experience of their GP practice as good in the 2026 GP Patient Survey.

Dr GWD Bhima recorded the highest result among the borough practices included in the comparison, with 96.2 per cent of respondents reporting a good overall experience. Milnrow Village Practice followed on 95.4 per cent, with The Village Medical Centre in Littleborough on 94 per cent.

At the other end of the comparison, Croft Shifa Health Centre recorded 44.9 per cent. The difference between the highest and lowest results was therefore 51.3 percentage points.

The England figure was 76.7 per cent.

EVERY ROCHDALE BOROUGH GP PRACTICE COMPARED

1. Dr GWD Bhima, Rochdale — 96.2%

2. Milnrow Village Practice, Milnrow and Newhey — 95.4%

3. The Village Medical Centre, Littleborough — 94.0%

4. Trinity Medical Centre, Littleborough — 92.6%

5. Birtle View Medical Practice, Heywood — 91.8%

6. The Kingsway Practice, Kingsway — 91.7%

7. Stonefield Street Surgery, Milnrow and Newhey — 90.4%

8. Pennine Surgery, Littleborough — 90.3%

9. The Hive Health Centre, Middleton — 88.9%

10. Family Practice, Middleton — 88.1%

11. Hopwood Medical Centre, Heywood — 87.7%

12. Littleborough Group Practice, Littleborough — 87.3%

13. Rochdale Road Medical Centre, Middleton — 86.7%

WHAT THE FIGURES SHOW

The results show substantial variation both across the borough and within individual townships. Heywood practices ranged from 91.8 per cent at Birtle View Medical Practice to 66.7 per cent at Heywood Health.

In Middleton, The Hive Health Centre recorded 88.9 per cent, compared with 71.9 per cent at Woodside Medical Centre.

The four Littleborough practices included in the comparison all recorded results above 87 per cent, with The Village Medical Centre leading the township on 94 per cent.

WHAT THE COMPARISON DOES NOT MEAN

The table compares practices on one patient-experience measure only. It is not a clinical-safety rating and does not assess diagnostic accuracy, prescribing, treatment outcomes or the performance of individual doctors.

The GP Patient Survey is based on a sample of registered patients, rather than every patient at each practice. Results are weighted, but smaller samples carry greater statistical uncertainty and practices serve populations with different needs and circumstances.

NHS England and Ipsos advise that the survey was not designed to create a definitive league table of GP practices. The ordering above is therefore a straightforward comparison of the published overall-experience percentage, not a declaration that one practice provides objectively better clinical care than another.

The 2026 survey was conducted between 2 January and 13 April and published on 9 July. Practices may have introduced changes since patients completed their questionnaires.

Rochdale Daily will invite practices to comment on their results and explain any improvements introduced since the survey period.

articles.title: Veterans invited to weekly breakfast club as Rochdale continues to support Armed Forces community
articles.excerpt: Military veterans from across Rochdale Borough are being encouraged to attend a free weekly breakfast club in Heywood, offering friendship, support and an opportunity to reconnect with fellow servicemen and women.
articles.content_html:
Military veterans from across Rochdale Borough are being invited to attend a weekly Armed Forces Breakfast Club held every Thursday morning at The Flying Horse Hotel in Heywood.

Supported by Rochdale Borough Council, the breakfast club has become a welcoming meeting place for former members of the Royal Navy, British Army and Royal Air Force. Breakfast is served between 9am and 10am every Thursday, with organisers reporting that thousands of breakfasts have now been served since the initiative began.

While the event offers a free breakfast, its real purpose is bringing veterans together. Leaving military service can often mean leaving behind the camaraderie and close friendships built over years of service. The breakfast club provides an opportunity to reconnect with fellow veterans, share experiences and offer informal peer support in a relaxed environment.

Rochdale has a proud military heritage stretching back generations. The borough has long been associated with the Lancashire Fusiliers and today remains home to a significant Armed Forces community, including serving personnel, reservists, veterans and military families. Many continue serving their communities long after leaving the military through volunteering, public service and local charities.

Research has consistently shown that social connection can play a vital role in improving wellbeing, particularly among veterans who may experience loneliness or find the transition to civilian life challenging. Community initiatives such as breakfast clubs provide an important opportunity to maintain friendships, reduce isolation and ensure no veteran feels forgotten.

The club is open to any military veteran, regardless of how long they served or when they left the Armed Forces. Whether someone completed a full career or served for only a short period, organisers say everyone who has worn the uniform is welcome.

The Armed Forces Breakfast Club takes place every Thursday between 9am and 10am at The Flying Horse Hotel, Heywood.

Rochdale has always been a borough that values those who have served. While remembrance services rightly honour military sacrifice each November, supporting veterans throughout the year is equally important. Initiatives such as the Heywood Breakfast Club demonstrate how something as simple as sharing breakfast can strengthen friendships, improve wellbeing and remind those who have served that their contribution continues to be appreciated by the community.

articles.title: Is this how the NHS treats its own? 81-year-old man left outside Rochdale Infirmary for ten hours
articles.excerpt: An 81-year-old man spent around ten hours lying outside Rochdale Infirmary while members of the public repeatedly sought help. Rochdale Daily investigates what happened and asks who held responsibility for his care.
articles.content_html:
An 81-year-old man lay confused, incoherent and unable to stand outside the grounds of Rochdale Infirmary for around ten hours while members of the public desperately tried to persuade the emergency services, hospital staff and social care agencies to help him.

The disturbing incident was witnessed and filmed by the editor of Rochdale Daily, who saw passers-by provide the man with water, blankets, cushions, food and cardboard while repeated attempts were made to establish which public service had responsibility for his welfare.

The man was found lying on the ground near the hospital car park. He appeared unable to stand unaided and could rarely string together more than two words. He later told those attempting to assist him that he was 81 years old.

Security staff were monitoring the situation and informed members of the public they had contacted Greater Manchester Police. Officers did not arrive until approximately ten hours after the ordeal began.

Members of the public repeatedly attempted to request an ambulance. During those calls, callers say they were informed the man was barred from the ambulance service because of previous behaviour and because of other matters that could not be discussed due to data protection legislation.

The precise legal status of any restriction involving the man has not yet been independently confirmed. However, Rochdale Daily holds video footage of the day's events, including numerous conversations between witnesses, members of the public and staff.

Whatever may have happened previously, the man lying on the ground that day appeared incapable of posing any immediate threat. He was confused, unable to stand, largely unable to communicate and repeatedly soiled himself while lying outside the hospital.

Members of the public also attempted to contact Rochdale Council Adult Social Care, people believed to be relatives, homelessness organisations and local charities. Appeals were placed on Facebook asking whether anyone knew the gentleman or could help locate family members.

Some comments on social media suggested the man had brought the situation upon himself if he had previously abused NHS staff. One commenter wrote: "You don't get barred from the NHS for nothing."

No one should minimise the abuse suffered by NHS workers. Nurses, doctors, paramedics, receptionists and security staff face unacceptable levels of violence, intimidation and verbal abuse every day. Staff deserve protection, and where individuals genuinely pose a danger, organisations are entitled to implement appropriate safeguards.

But that was not the man witnessed by Rochdale Daily.

For hour after hour he remained lying on the ground, unable to stand, struggling to communicate and apparently incapable of caring for himself. Members of the public did not witness any aggression towards staff, security or those trying to help him.

Throughout the day, ambulance vehicles entered and left the hospital site. Witnesses attempted to flag them down, but the vehicles continued past. Others reportedly stopped only to explain they were unable to assist.

Approximately six hours into the incident, two nurses accompanied by hospital security entered the car park and spoke with those attempting to help the man.

According to the editor's contemporaneous video recording, the nurses stated they could not treat the gentleman unless the situation became a matter of "life or death".

When asked what 'life or death' would look like to an untrained member of the public, they replied: "We couldn't tell you."

Members of the public then asked whose duty of care the gentleman fell under if he died while no organisation would intervene. One member of staff replied: "Not you."

When pressed as to which organisation would carry responsibility if treatment continued to be refused, those present say no clear answer was given.

One nurse then stated that the gentleman's breathing would have to stop before intervention could take place.

The editor replied that she could not see him breathing. The nurse looked over the wall towards the gentleman and responded that his chest was rising and therefore he was breathing.

During the exchange, one nurse was recorded saying: "This is what you get when you're on it day and night."

When asked what she meant by the remark, no explanation was given.

Later in the incident, a person identifying themselves as a family member stated the gentleman had dementia. Rochdale Daily has not independently verified that relationship or medical diagnosis.

A representative from Get Together After Serving CIC attended the scene after becoming aware of the incident and also attempted to secure medical assistance.

The representative said they were informed the gentleman was subject to a restraining order involving the Northern Care Alliance NHS Foundation Trust and that members of the public would need to transport him outside the area before treatment could be sought elsewhere.

Rochdale Daily has requested clarification from the Trust regarding that alleged restriction.

Throughout the ordeal, members of the public continued caring for the gentleman. Bottles of water, blankets, cushions, cardboard and food were brought to make him more comfortable while people searched desperately for someone willing to take responsibility.

Among the organisations contacted, only Get Together After Serving CIC and Hebron Pentecostal Church attended to assist.

Approximately ten hours after the incident began, police officers attended the scene.

The following morning, disposable cups, bowls and cardboard still marked the place where the elderly man had spent much of the previous day.

This investigation is not an argument that NHS staff should tolerate abuse. They should not. Nor is it an argument that previous violent or abusive behaviour should simply be ignored.

It is, however, a question of safeguarding.

If an elderly man is confused, apparently incapable of caring for himself, unable to stand, repeatedly soiling himself and lying outside the grounds of a hospital, who has responsibility for protecting him?

If previous behaviour has resulted in restrictions, what emergency pathway exists when that same individual later appears to lack capacity or requires urgent medical assessment?

Those are questions Northern Care Alliance NHS Foundation Trust, North West Ambulance Service, Greater Manchester Police and Rochdale Council's Adult Social Care service should now answer.

Rochdale Daily has contacted all relevant organisations for comment and will publish their responses in full when received.

Until then, one unavoidable question remains.

Is this how the NHS treats its own?

articles.title: Peaceful Pool sessions return to Whitworth Leisure & Wellbeing Centre for SEND families
articles.excerpt: Whitworth Leisure & Wellbeing Centre is once again offering its popular Peaceful Pool sessions throughout the summer holidays, creating a calm, welcoming and sensory-friendly swimming environment for children and adults with SEND and their families.
articles.content_html:
Families across the Rossendale Valley and Rochdale borough are being invited to enjoy a quieter, more inclusive swimming experience this summer as Whitworth Leisure & Wellbeing Centre continues its popular Peaceful Pool sessions.

Designed specifically for children and adults with Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND), along with their families, the sessions provide a calm, judgement-free environment where everyone can relax, connect and enjoy time together at their own pace.

The initiative recognises that many families can find busy public swimming sessions overwhelming due to noise, bright lighting and sensory stimulation. Peaceful Pool aims to remove those barriers by creating an environment where participants feel comfortable, supported and included.

Sessions will take place every Thursday from 11:30am until 1:00pm throughout the six-week summer holidays.

To create a more accessible experience, the pool environment will feature reduced lighting to provide a calmer atmosphere, while sensory toys and floating aids will be available for swimmers to enjoy. Families are encouraged to use the facilities in whatever way feels right for them, whether that means swimming, playing in the water, paddling at the poolside or simply becoming familiar with the environment.

Organisers say the sessions are all about allowing people to be themselves without fear of judgement.

The promotional campaign explains that many families of children with SEND can often feel judged or cautious about how their child's behaviour may be perceived in public spaces. Peaceful Pool has therefore been designed to offer a welcoming environment where everyone can feel safe, respected and accepted.

The centre's message is simple: 'Everyone is welcome here just as you are.' That philosophy reflects a growing recognition across the leisure sector of the importance of making public facilities more inclusive and accessible for people with additional needs.

Swimming is widely recognised for its physical and mental wellbeing benefits, helping to improve confidence, mobility, coordination and overall fitness while providing an enjoyable activity for the whole family. Creating opportunities for families to access those benefits in a supportive environment can make a significant difference for many people who may otherwise struggle to attend mainstream sessions.

The Peaceful Pool sessions are available at the standard swim admission price, ensuring families can take part without paying a premium for accessible provision.

Whitworth Leisure & Wellbeing Centre continues to expand its programme of community-focused activities, with Peaceful Pool forming part of its wider commitment to ensuring local leisure facilities are welcoming and inclusive for residents of all ages and abilities.

Peaceful Pool takes place every Thursday between 11:30am and 1:00pm throughout the six-week summer holidays at Whitworth Leisure & Wellbeing Centre.

articles.title: One man became one walk – now Rochdale's Men Walking and Talking group hopes others will join him
articles.excerpt: A new Men Walking and Talking group has launched in Rochdale, offering men a safe, informal place to meet, walk and talk as organisers hope to tackle loneliness, improve mental wellbeing and reduce the stigma surrounding men's mental health.
articles.content_html:
A simple walk can sometimes be the first step towards changing a life.

That's the message behind Men Walking and Talking, the national Community Interest Company helping men support one another through conversation, companionship and fresh air. The organisation recently launched its Rochdale group, offering a free weekly walk where men can meet without pressure, judgement or the expectation that they have to talk if they don't want to. The walks take place every Thursday evening from Rochdale Cenotaph and are open to all men, with no booking required.

The Rochdale group's organiser recently reflected on one of the challenges facing any new community initiative – sometimes the first person to turn up is the organiser themselves. In recent weeks he has often found himself walking alone, but says he'll continue turning up each Thursday because he believes someone who needs the group will eventually come.

That quiet determination reflects the purpose of Men Walking and Talking. The organisation was founded on the belief that men often find it easier to open up while walking side by side than sitting face-to-face. There is no expectation to share personal struggles, but there is always the opportunity to chat if someone feels ready.

Research has consistently shown that regular physical activity can play an important role in supporting mental wellbeing. Walking outdoors has been linked to reduced symptoms of anxiety and depression, lower stress levels and improved mood. Spending time in nature, exercising regularly and building social connections can all contribute positively to mental health, while loneliness and social isolation are recognised risk factors for poor mental wellbeing.

For many men, however, talking about mental health remains difficult. Although attitudes have improved in recent years, stigma still prevents some people from seeking support. Organisations such as Men Walking and Talking aim to break down those barriers by creating informal spaces where conversation develops naturally rather than feeling like therapy.

The need for initiatives like this remains significant. Suicide continues to be one of the leading causes of death among men under the age of 50 in the UK, with men accounting for around three-quarters of all registered suicides nationally. Behind every statistic are families, friends and communities left dealing with unimaginable loss.

Groups such as Men Walking and Talking cannot replace professional mental health services, but they can provide something equally valuable – connection. A friendly face, a shared walk and the knowledge that someone else understands can make a real difference for people who may otherwise feel isolated.

Community is another important part of the group's mission. Beyond improving physical fitness, regular walks help people build friendships, strengthen local networks and create a sense of belonging. Many participants across the country say they first attended for the walk but kept returning because of the people they met along the way.

The Rochdale organiser hopes more local men will consider giving the group a try. There is no membership, no pressure to speak and no expectation to explain why you've come. Whether someone wants to chat openly, listen quietly or simply enjoy an evening walk with others, they are welcome.

If you are struggling with your mental health, you do not have to face it alone. If you are having thoughts of suicide or feel unable to keep yourself safe, call 999 immediately or go to your nearest Accident and Emergency department. You can also contact Samaritans free of charge on 116 123, email jo@samaritans.org, or reach out to CALM (Campaign Against Living Miserably) on 0800 58 58 58 or through its webchat service. If your situation is not an emergency but you need support, speak to your GP or contact NHS 111 for advice.

Sometimes the hardest part is taking the first step. For one Rochdale volunteer, that first step has meant walking alone while waiting for others to join him. He hopes that, before long, those solitary walks will become conversations shared with men who simply needed someone to walk beside.
